place-work.text: Masonry, smaller habitation spaces, food evidence and built alignments reveal different kinds of work. Regional organization remains interpreted, while a dated Pueblo council statement establishes living significance without identifying every ancient institution or implying assent to this account.

name: Chaco: building, gathering and continuing histories
place: Chaco Canyon, San Juan Basin, New Mexico, United States
geographicPrecision: Pueblo Bonito site locator. The regional Chacoan system extended beyond this point; no fixed political border is drawn.

interval.label: Selected Chaco regional context, c. 850–1250 CE
interval.note: Regional frame. Pueblo Bonito construction c850–1150 and changes in the 1100s/1200s are distinct; this endpoint does not end Pueblo peoples or their ties to Chaco.

question: What connects a stone building, a traded ingredient and a living cultural landscape?
summary: Chaco’s buildings required stonework, timber, food and repeated care. Great houses, smaller habitation compounds and constructed alignments reveal different scales of work. Their institutional meaning remains debated, while a dated Pueblo council statement makes continuing relationships with the landscape explicit.

sections.title: Materials made different spaces possible
sections.text: Rows of stones and wood spanning openings are visible in the supplied Pueblo Bonito photograph. The NPS architectural account describes great-house walls built with rubble cores and carefully coursed outer masonry. These were different parts of a construction, not simply a decorated flat surface. Builders also arranged rooms, plazas and circular spaces. Pueblo Bonito’s staged construction frame stretches approximately 850–1150 CE: making a large building involved successive work rather than one completed moment. The photograph cannot date every part or name its builders.

sections.title: Smaller houses belong beside the monuments
sections.text: The same NPS account describes smaller habitation sites with storage rooms, pithouses, outdoor shelters and later room additions. Such spaces place keeping supplies and carrying out household activities beside monumental construction. Their smaller scale matters: a great house should not stand in for every home in the canyon. NPS discusses the great houses as possible public architecture used for gathering and ceremony. That interpretation opens a question about how residents and visitors shared work; it does not recover every room’s function or choose one settled government model.

sections.title: Food connected fields, storage and gathering
sections.text: People living and gathering in this landscape needed food as well as buildings. The NPS subsistence account discusses rainfall variation, stored plant remains and water-control features. It presents competing explanations for the balance between local cultivation and supplies brought from outside. Directing seasonal water, keeping crops and preparing food were practical tasks; their precise scale and organization remain questions. A material found in selected vessels can document an ingredient, while evidence for staple farming must address different fields, samples and environmental conditions.

sections.title: Built connections have more than one possible use
sections.text: Carved steps, masonry stairways and ramps show work invested in moving through the landscape. NPS also explains that many identified road segments do not form a demonstrably continuous route. Some may have had ceremonial or symbolic roles alongside practical uses. New construction and Chaco’s regional role changed in the 1100s and 1200s; this does not end Pueblo histories. A 2025 All Pueblo Council of Governors resolution describes continuing spiritual, historical and cultural significance. It is an attributed statement of living relationships, not proof that every person endorses one archaeological explanation.

deeperReading.title: A photograph contains preservation history
deeperReading.text: The surviving walls need care after exposure. NPS describes water, freeze–thaw cycles and lost roofs or plaster as causes of deterioration. Modern treatment can include mortar repair, replacement stones, capping and backfilling. Its account also documents local Navajo crews working in the late 1930s preservation programme. These are skilled activities with their own dates. They make the present photograph useful evidence of a conserved structure, without letting us classify every visible stone as ancient or modern by appearance alone.

deeperReading.title: A small chemical sample does not become a universal menu
deeperReading.text: The retained Crown and Hurst consultation records five vessel-fragment samples from Pueblo Bonito. Three probable cylinder-jar samples yielded theobromine, interpreted as cacao evidence; stylistic dating places the sherds around 1000–1125 CE. This supports an ingredient-use inference and raises questions about preparation and movement. It does not identify all intermediaries, an exact route, every household’s access or the main source of staple calories. The study’s separately copyrighted vessel figure is not reproduced.

deeperReading.title: Institutional descriptions need named perspectives
deeperReading.text: A gathering place, a redistribution centre and a political centre are interpretations that call for different evidence. They need not explain every structure or century alike. The council resolution contributes another kind of record: a dated statement that Greater Chaco remains culturally significant. Reading it alongside archaeological questions neither makes contemporary peoples disappear at a timeline boundary nor treats them as unanimous witnesses to one reconstruction. Fuller specialist and community review remains necessary.

evidenceReading.title: Visible work, chemical traces and a dated community statement
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of different sources. A photograph, a small analytical sample and a community-authored document answer different questions; none is a complete census or a recovered route.

items.label: Masonry faces are visible; the whole building system is interpreted
items.text: The supplied photograph shows arranged stone courses and wood over openings. NPS separately describes rubble-core/faced masonry and modern conservation treatments.
items.interpretation: The photograph supports close observation of materials and arrangement. It does not expose every core, identify all modern repairs, restore missing floors or establish each room’s use, occupants or original construction year.

items.label: Three positive samples support a bounded ingredient inference
items.text: The earlier checked 2009 study tested fragments representing five vessels; three probable cylinder jars yielded theobromine, interpreted as cacao evidence.
items.interpretation: Presence in these samples is not evidence of universal access, a fixed serving event, an exact route or a field’s crop yield. The actual earlier 27 October consultation is retained; the 29 October consultation did not reread inaccessible full text or reproduce its separately copyrighted figure.

items.label: A council speaks about continuing significance
items.text: Page 1 of APCG 2025-02 describes Greater Chaco’s continuing spiritual, historical and cultural significance to many Pueblos and Tribes including Hopi.
items.interpretation: This is a dated community-authored statement about living relationships. It does not date a wall, represent each individual’s view, establish current law or imply community assent to this atlas or one archaeological interpretation.

familyActivity.title: What work can a wall help us explain?
steps: Find rows of differently sized stones and wood spanning an opening in the supplied photograph. Describe what is visible before naming a room’s purpose.
Read the source capsule with an adult if useful. Make three cards: visible construction, a chemical finding and a dated community statement. Match each claim to its kind of evidence.
Write one supported sentence about a building task. Add a question about a room’s use or an ingredient’s route that the photograph cannot answer.
Explain why a selected timeline endpoint does not show that Pueblo peoples or their relationships with Chaco ended.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: NPS describes great-house masonry with cores and faced stonework, alongside smaller habitation/storage compounds and modern preservation. The earlier checked Crown/Hurst study reports three positive probable cylinder-jar samples among five tested vessel fragments, not a universal drink or exact route. APCG 2025-02 p. 1 describes Chaco’s continuing cultural significance. Stone courses can be observed; hidden cores, ingredient identification and contemporary statements require their respective sources. None names every builder or proves one room’s use.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian, archaeologist or community approval
review.scope: Selected NPS accounts, the retained cacao consultation, a council statement and an 1850 ruin plan support this layered inquiry. Earlier case dates, image bytes and dated source scopes remain.
limitations: NPS c.700–1300, Pueblo Bonito c.850–1150, the 850–1250 case and c.1000–1125 sample dates are separate conventions, not a lifespan for Pueblo peoples.
Food supply, water works and regional institutions remain debated. Earlier NPS typologies do not establish a universal household model, political hierarchy, census or crop yield.

Cacao retains its 27 October consultation. Fresh cacao/isotope access challenges and USGS/2012 food-source failures supplied no new complete methods, figures or crop-provenance review. Detailed access scopes remain in the bibliography.

APCG 2025-02 was consulted at p.1/header/first two WHEREAS clauses and selected page pixels only. It supplies an attributed statement, not current-law verification, universal agreement or approval of this atlas. No logo or figure reused.
Discontinuous alignments and interpreted functions do not recover an exact road, border or timber convoy. No route between the inquiry’s stops or new numeric locator is supplied.

The unchanged doorway photo has unknown exposure date, individual maker and current remote-original parity. Pixels do not date individual repairs. Separately credited NPS-hosted images retain separate rights.

The 1850 ruin record has no measured scale bar or single ancient phase. Underlying-public-domain and provider CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 notices remain distinct; no tracing. The direct Rumsey item and full volume were not read.
Independent scholarly/community review, real family use, human screen-reader, physical-device and physical-print acceptance remain open.
